output:
Monsieur l'Inspecteur,

I write before you return, so that you have this in my own words and not in the town's.

In the spring of 1889 I attended Jules Monnier in his last illness. He suffered badly at night, and I gave him laudanum for it. On one bad night I raised the dose too far, and he died before morning. I certified the cause as failure of the heart. That was not a false diagnosis of what stopped his heart, and no one asked me for more. I have kept that silence for eleven years and have been civil to his family throughout.

In December Aurèle found his brother's last letter among the papers he was sorting for the new century. It described the doses. On Sunday, in the hall before dinner, he showed it to me and told me that at midnight he would tell Félix, and afterwards the authorities. "At the turn of the century I settle my accounts." He was not angry. He had decided.

After dinner I played piquet with Odile in the salon. At twenty-three minutes past ten I rose, said I would fetch my cigars, and asked her to play for me. The piano would cover my steps. I went up to the atelier and passed the library door, which was shut.

Lina had been sent down. Aurèle was at his bench under the long windows with the repeater in his hand. I spoke to him. He would not change his mind. I struck him once from behind with the brass mallet from his bench. As he fell he pressed the slide, and I heard it: ten low notes, two doubled, eight high. I counted them as anyone in this town would count them. Ten thirty-eight.

I stopped the regulator and moved its hands back to five minutes past ten, an hour when I had been at cards with Odile in full view of the room. I came down, took my cigar case from my coat in the hall, and was back in the salon at six minutes to eleven. Odile stopped playing when I came in. The hall clock struck eleven a moment later.

When you asked me, I told you I had gone out at a quarter to eleven by my watch, after the repeater would have sounded. That was the one lie I told you. I did not know that Félix had heard the strike from below, or that Girard had heard it from the street, or that the kitchen had heard the piano begin. I should have reckoned on the house. A house of this kind keeps its own time.

I have no defence you would accept, and I will not offer one. I was fond of Aurèle for thirty years. Each year at dinner he told me my watch ran fast. It did.

Odile did not know. Please tell her so, and tell her that the choice was mine alone.

Casimir Vauthier

La Chaux-de-Fonds, 1 January 1900, at dawn
